title: Introduction
text:
Organizing Principles
The structure of this book parallels project sequence. The more traditional presentation of Psychometrics is organized by fundamental concepts. This was a deliberate choice and intended to better serve the developer of psychological assessments.
The content is informed by the current literature on Psychological measurement (e.g., Borsboom, 2022) as well as important foundational sources (e.g., Stevens, 1946) and one guiding “North Star”, the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educational Research Association and American Psychological Association and National Council on Measurement in Education, 2014). We have made every effort to, where appropriate, link the current book material to corresponding Standards within the forthcoming edition (edition 8).
By tradition, the development of a measure is aligned with one predominant philosophical orientation, although analytical explorations are often conducted via the application of multiple orientations. This is smart, as multiple investigations from multiple angles should provide the most information regarding the effectiveness of a measure. We have tried to be careful about our use of the words “tradition” and “philosophy” such that “tradition” is a categorical label whereas “philosophy” connotes more meaningful differences in thought or specification regarding the nature of measurement.
Consistent with this, “diversity of traditions is good” perspective1, we take an atypical route toward presentation and integration of different psychometric traditions – we separate psychometric traditions (classical test theory, item response theory, network psychometrics) from the procedures often tied to those traditions.
This will likely be the most controversial structural decision we have made, although it is again aligned with the needs of the practitioner (test developer and analyst), who should be provided multiple options (aka procedures) for any one investigation (aka analysis). The consequential, philosophical orientations of each tradition is handled separately, in 2  Psychometric Philosophies.

title: 2  Psychometric Philosophies
text:
2.1 Classical Test Theory
The belief that we have the capability to measure the abstract and theoretical similarly to the concrete and physical most likely started (or at least is widely acknowledged as starting) with Francis Galton, who predated “Psychology” but had an interest in individual differences (Galton, 1883). Later esteemed contributors to early Psychology such as Edward Lee Thorndike and James McKeen Cattell held similar opinions (Cattell, 1890; Thorndike, 1904, 1918), although others, such as Alfred Binet, expressed more skepticism regarding the capabilities of Psychological measurement (Binet, 1898).
Philosophies, within the context of Psychometrics, reflect theoretical beliefs regarding the nature of measurement. One of these beliefs is held tight, as an orthodoxy, such that empirical associations contrary to the orthodoxy are deemed heretical and violations of measurement (Rasch measurement – covered in Section 2.4). Most philosophies, however, take less extreme positions regarding the nature of measurement. All share a dependence on individual differences.
It is useful for you to align yourself with one of these philosophical orientations from the perspective of assessment development. You should, however, borrow investigative procedures from each of these traditions to evaluate the quality of your measure (after all, each isolated philosophy has its own unique strengths and weaknesses).
We will present four philosophical orientations (see Table 2.1), although these are not intended to represent a comprehensive or exhaustive listing. Again, being cautious with terminology, we refer to the theoretical perspective on measurement as a philosophical orientation whereas the holder of that orientation is referred to as a tradition.1 There are, no doubt, useful perspectives on the nature of measurement that have not yet been explicitly articulated or widely disseminated and the field is yet in need of perspectives that might help explain some persistently vexing mysteries…
CTT came first (Edgeworth, 1888; Spearman, 1904) – there was a flurry of activity in the 1950’s and 1960’s that challenged and/or augmented CTT with Generalizability Theory, IRT, and Rasch measurement (Cronbach et al., 1963; Lord, 1952; Lord & Novick, 1968; Rasch, 1960). Then the deep thinking about measurement laid largely dormant until Network Psychometrics (Borsboom & Cramer, 2013).
Although the same philosophical orientation within educational contexts is referred to as True Score Theory (TST), the Standards (as well as the broader social and behavioral sciences) have preferred to refer to this perspective on measurement as Classical Test Theory (CTT)2 (American Educational Research Association and American Psychological Association and National Council on Measurement in Education, 2014). This orientation has the longest history of specification and application (Gulliksen, 1950) and unquestionably remains dominant in casual academic (e.g., non–Psychometrician) conceptualization of Psychological measurement.
The framework of CTT is built on three fundamental concepts:
and the most concise articulation of CTT simply specifies the algebraic form of relationship between the three concepts:
\[X = T + e \tag{2.1}\]
The observed score, \(X\), is the traditional focus of practical attention for any measurement practitioner. The observed score is also referred to (synonymously) as a raw score. To best comprehend \(X\), you should also consider it to be synonymous with an aggregate scale score3. \(X\) is tangible. It is directly observable and quantifiable. When a student completes a 10–item mathematics exam and correctly answers 7 items, this student’s \(X\) is 74.
Of course the instructor interprets the student’s score, \(X\)=7, as an indication of the student’s knowledge of math. The student, however, may quibble with the interpretation and claim that their knowledge is greater5 – this brings us to a second CTT component, \(e\).
\(e\) represents the concept of error. There are two conceptually distinct types of error that CTT adherents acknowledge: random error (\(e_{r}\)) and systematic error (\(e_{s}\)).
The minimal CTT equation, \(X=T+e\), is most centrally concerned with random error, so we could rewrite the equation thusly: \[X = T + e_{r} \tag{2.2}\]
Equation 2.1 and Equation 2.2 are considered equivalent canonical6 specifications of CTT. Guion (2011) has proposed a third alternative (Equation 2.3) that more explicitly accomodates \(e_{s}\), although this is NOT generally accepted as a canonical articulation of CTT. The (important) distinctions and similarities between \(e_{s}\) and \(e_{r}\), including the Guion (2011) reformulation of the CTT formula, will be discussed in XXXXX.
\[X = s + e \tag{2.3}\]
The third CTT component, \(T\), is a concept that only exists in the theoretical realm. \(T\) represents a person’s true score – their actual state of being with respect to the focal construct of interest7. For example, a student’s ACTUAL, REAL, TRUE knowledge of math.
\(T\) assumes that every person has a true location of construct standing along whatever construct is the focus of Psychometric attention. \(T\) is independent of any administered exam. We (mere mortal Psychometricians) have no special access to \(T\), we can only infer an individual’s \(T\) through behavioral indicators – one very germane indicator (we hope) is that individual’s score, \(X\), on a Psychological assessment.
To the extent that error, \(e\), is minimal, \(X\) will provide a good approximation of \(T\). If error grows, our inference that \(X\) is an adequate representation of \(T\) becomes more dubious. Of course as Psychometricians, we don’t often apply a word such as “dubious” (even though it is entirely appropriate and descriptive) – rather, we prefer, by tradition, more specific terms such as reliability and validity (these topics are covered in XXXXX and XXXXX).

title: 2  Psychometric Philosophies
text:
2.2 Generalizability Theory
An extension/liberalization of Classical Test Theory developed by Cronbach and colleagues in the 1960’s (Cronbach et al., 1963, 1972; Gleser et al., 1965; Rajaratnam et al., 1965). Uses analysis of variance (ANOVA) to partition multiple sources of error variance (“facets” such as items, raters, occasions, forms) rather than a single error term. Distinguishes universe scores, generalizability coefficients (for relative decisions), and dependability coefficients (for absolute decisions). Supports G-studies (estimating variance components) and D-studies (optimizing designs). Better handles complex measurement situations than basic CTT.

title: 2  Psychometric Philosophies
text:
2.3 Item Response Theory
A popular alternative to CTT focuses relatively greater philosophical attention on the item and underlying latent trait. Early contributions were from Lord (1952) and Lord & Novick (1968). The interaction of each item with the respondent is central here and specified via a probablistic model8.

2.3.1 Grok (5/16/26)
Framing IRT as a measurement philosophy in a psychometrics text is an excellent opportunity to elevate the discussion beyond technical models and position IRT as a fundamental shift in how we think about psychological measurement. Here are targeted suggestions for structuring and writing that section.


2.3.2 Suggested Section Title Options

“Item Response Theory as a Measurement Philosophy”
“IRT: From Test Scores to Latent Trait Measurement”
“The IRT Paradigm: A Probabilistic Approach to Psychological Measurement”
“Beyond Classical Test Theory: IRT’s Philosophy of Invariant, Individual-Focused Measurement”



2.3.3 Recommended Structure

Opening Hook / Historical-Conceptual Bridge (1–2 pages)
Start by contrasting IRT with the approaches your readers already know (e.g., the Thurstone and Likert methods you asked about earlier).

Classical Test Theory (CTT) and early scaling methods treat the test (or total score) as the primary unit of analysis.

IRT treats the item–person interaction as the fundamental unit and views observed responses as probabilistic manifestations of an underlying latent trait (θ).
Example framing:
> “While Thurstone’s attitude scales and Likert’s summative scoring advanced attitude measurement, they remained rooted in a test-centric, linear, and sample-dependent logic. Item Response Theory offers a different philosophy: measurement should be grounded in explicit, falsifiable models of how individuals interact with individual items along a latent continuum.”

Core Philosophical Principles (the heart of the section)
Explicitly articulate IRT’s worldview. Key pillars to cover:

Latent trait ontology: Psychological constructs (ability, attitude, personality traits, etc.) are continuous, unobservable variables. Responses are observable indicators whose probability is a mathematical function of person location (θ) and item parameters.

Probabilistic rather than deterministic measurement: Responses are not fixed; they are governed by an item response function (IRF / ICC). This acknowledges uncertainty and error at the item level.

Invariance as a core goal: Item parameters should be (largely) independent of the sample of persons, and person parameters independent of the specific items (when the model fits). This is a stronger form of measurement objectivity than CTT typically provides.

Item-level focus and information: Every item contributes differently depending on where a person stands on the trait. Measurement precision can vary across the trait continuum and can be engineered.

Conjoint measurement / parameter separation: The ideal (especially in Rasch models) is to separate person and item influences in a way that supports fundamental measurement properties (e.g., specific objectivity).

Unidimensionality and local independence assumptions as theoretical commitments rather than mere statistical checks.

IRT as a Paradigm Shift
Use a clean comparison table (highly recommended for textbooks):








Aspect
Classical Test Theory (CTT)
Item Response Theory (IRT)




Unit of analysis
Total test score
Individual item responses


Model type
Linear, additive
Nonlinear, probabilistic


Sample dependence
High (item statistics vary by group)
Low (invariant parameters when model holds)


Precision of measurement
Single SEM for the whole test
Varies by trait level (test information function)


Score interpretation
Norm-referenced, relative
Trait-referenced, absolute on latent scale


Adaptive testing
Difficult
Natural fit


Philosophy
Test as a random sample of items
Explicit model of response process



Implications for Practice and Theory

Test construction becomes item-bank oriented rather than fixed-form.

Scoring can be individual and adaptive.

Validity evidence is strengthened through item fit, differential item functioning (DIF), and scale information.

Links to broader measurement theory (e.g., representational vs. operationalist philosophies, or Rasch’s specific objectivity).

Limitations and ongoing debates: model–data fit requirements, choice between dominance vs. ideal-point models (especially for personality/attitudes), philosophical critiques of latent variables.

Closing Transition
End by foreshadowing technical chapters: “This philosophical foundation sets the stage for the specific IRT models (Rasch/1PL, 2PL, 3PL, graded response, etc.) that operationalize these principles.”



2.3.4 Writing Style and Pedagogical Tips

Use accessible language first, then formalize. Start with an everyday analogy (e.g., “measuring height with a ruler whose markings change depending on who is using it” vs. a stable metric scale).

Include a simple visual of an Item Characteristic Curve early — it embodies the philosophy.

Reference foundational works: Lord & Novick (1968), Rasch (1960), Embretson & Reise (2000), Hambleton et al., and key papers on measurement philosophy (e.g., discussions of conjoint measurement, invariance).

Pose rhetorical questions: “What does it mean to truly ‘measure’ an attitude or ability?”

Keep the tone reflective rather than purely technical — this is the “why” chapter.

This framing positions IRT not as “just another set of models” but as a coherent measurement philosophy that aspires to stronger scientific properties than its predecessors. It flows naturally from your earlier coverage of Thurstone and Likert while preparing readers for the mathematical details to come.


2.3.5 Dominance models
Dominance models, such as the GRM, assume a monotonically increasing relationship between the latent trait level and the probability of selecting a higher response category on an item (e.g., on a Likert scale). This contrasts with unfolding or ideal point models, where the response function is non-monotonic and peaks at a point matching the respondent’s trait level. 1–, 2–, 3–point logistic models (1PL, 2PL, 3PL), Graded Response Model, Partial Credit Model


2.3.6 Ideal point models
Frequently estimated via the Generalized Graded Unfolding Model [GGUM; Roberts et al. (2000)]

title: 3  Types of Assessment
text:
3.1 Characteristics
A fundamentally important distinction exists between two qualitatively different types of assessment. If assessment responses can be reasonably categorized as correct or incorrect, you are dealing with a test (see also Note 3.1). If assessment responses are not intended to be interpreted as correct and incorrect, the assessment should be referred to as an inventory. There are many meaningful differences between (true) tests and inventories (see Section 3.1), but the most consequential is that (true) tests are subject to different sources of error than are Psychological inventories.
The Standards treat the subordinate word “test” as being synonymous with the superordinate term “assessment”. This is an unfortunate legacy concession and most likely the result of “serving multiple masters yet satisfying none”. The Standards is a resource meant to be applicable across disciplines. Within educational contexts, the semantic distinction is unnecessary (the assessments in education are almost universally true tests). Psychologists, however, should always be careful in their communications – if the measure is intended to reflect correct and incorrect, it is a test. If scores are not intended to convey correct or incorrect, it is an inventory.

title: Scale Development
text:
Construct definition (conceptual)
The word “scale” has several meanings within measurement contexts. Scales of measurement refer to categorical strata defined by rules governing the assignment of numbers to things (e.g., Stevens, 1946). Aggregate summaries of responses across multiple indicators are most often referred to as scale scores, and these are further dissociated as either raw– or standard–scale scores. “Scale development” refers to the process of operationalizing your measure. This is the focus of the current chapter.

title: Scale Development
text:
Measure adequacy (empirical)
Empirical estimates of your measure’s adequacy (extent to which it is a reasonable operationalization of your conceptual construct) are only limited by your creativity, but by tradition are categorized as indices of reliability and validity – each of which has several possible estimation procedures. It should also be noted that the constructs of reliability and validity exhibit a high degree of overlap. In the context of several different discussions regarding content validity, said:

Perhaps instead of content validity we should call it content reliability, or job sample reliability. Perhaps we should, but I doubt that we will. Verbal habits are not tha teasy to change. We are no doubt fated to live henceforth with somewhat imprecise terminology, and with the confused thinking about test quality it is likely to spawn (Ebel (1975), quoted in Guion (1977))


Content validation – not currently located anywhere.
This is the “evaluation of operational definitions” (Guion (1977), p. 6)

people who talk about content validity are talking about how well a small sample of behavior observed in the measurement procedure represents the whole class of behavior that falls within the boundaries defining the content domain. This content representativeness is explicitly what people are talking about when they speak of content validity (Guion (1977), p. 3)

Anderson & Gerbing (1991) speak of substantive validity as a subordinate aspect of construct validity, although this term has not realized broad adoption and the Anderson & Gerbing (1991) method is more commonly conceptualized as a content validation procedure.
Lawshe (1975)’s content validity ratio was, for many years, the most popular index of content validity:
\[
CVR = \frac{n_e - \frac{N}{2}}{\frac{N}{2}}
\tag{1}\]
Lawshe (1975) asked a content evaluation panel to independently rate each items in terms of being, 1) Essential, 2) Useful but not essential, or 3) Not necessary. Lawshe (1975)’s initial presentation was focused on jobs, and his process
The content validity coefficient here was operationalized as a quantification of consensus (among the panel constituents; see Equation 1). \(n_e\) is the number of panelists who rated an item essential. \(N\) is the total number of judges on the panel. The CVR will be negative if less than half of panelists rule an item essential and positive if more than half agree that an item is essential.
Hinkin & Tracey (1999) Colquitt et al. (2019)

I do like to speak sensibly, and I dislike further corrupting the language, but I don’t know what else to call them. (p. 5)

title: 5  Domain Sampling
text:
There is a difference between dominance (e.g., Likert, 1932) and ideal point (e.g., Thurstone, 1928) methods of scale construction, and this difference must be acknowledged when crafting indicators1. The dominance model assumes that “more” of a trait within the respondent drives more extreme responses to trait indicators. The ideal point requires indicators to be sampled from representative locations all along the trait continuum. There has been some debate regarding which approach is less problematic (Drasgow et al., 2010; e.g., Oswald & Schell, 2010). The ideal point approach is most closely aligned with IRT and Rasch philosophies, although it also “works” with CTT.
Our suggestion is:
We borrow from both perspectives and recommend… If you intend to evaluate your measure from the perspective of IRT or Rasch, then items targeted at different trait levels become more practically important (e.g., you should endeavor to oversample items at many different plausible trait points).

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.1 Title page
Documentation of your psychometrics project occurs within a technical report (aka “tech report”). The technical report contains, at a minimum:
Your goal within the technical report is exacting descriptive communication of the development and investigation of psychometric properties of your focal measure. You should apply whatever writing level is best suited to convey your thoughts with the highest level of descriptive integrity. Any anticipated reading–level limitations of how you communicate technical report information should not restrain your documentation. It is okay to assume a post–baccalaureate reading level – aka individuals who have similar advanced training as yours. Additional measure–relevant documentation in the form of white papers, local validation studies, and marketing material should be treated differently and target a general consumer audience (7th–grade reading level), but it is ok for your technical report to be “technical”.
Regarding the structure of your report, you are free to use style guidelines (such as those offered by APA (American Psychological Association, 2020) or MLA (Modern Language Association of America, 2021)), but you should not in any way feel constrained by these. The content of your technical report should reflect the elements discussed in this chapter (see also Important 9.1), but the format should reflect some uniqueness of the authors. Have some fun with the format – use icons, images, and even (non–wacky) fonts with restrained abandon. You may even want to consult a friend who has experience with graphic design or other artistic ventures. The look and feel should reflect YOU (or the organization you represent), not some stodgy arbiter of margin dimensions or running head structure.
The remainder of Chapter 9 focuses on each element of your technical report separately. The entirety of your report is merely an aggregation of these individual elements, although you should give greatest weight (in terms of page space and descriptive detail) to information contained in Section 9.5 and Section 9.6.
The title page may also be referred to as a “cover page” – we are considering these terms synonymous for the purposes of a technical report. This represents, with traditional hard–copy reports, the first impression of your project. Branding is important here – if you are representing an organization, there may be a pre–existing preferred format or structure. If you are representing yourself, think about not just this current project, but also future projects that you may wish to conduct. Once you decide on a styling, it is best to stick with it across future projects.

text:
9.3 Table of contents








Figure 9.3: Example cutely formatted table of contents



You may choose to include the table of contents prior to your executive summary or after your executive summary. We construct our tech reports with the title page first, executive summary second, and table of contents third, but the order of presentation of these two elements can be determined by personal preference. Like the title page, you may be creative with the table of contents. If your report is generated in a format that permits, provide hyperlinks to component sections within the table of contents itself. You may choose to make the table of contents omnipresent (as we have done with this book – look to your left!!! ), but even if you do so, still include a static table of contents near the “beginning” of your report.

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.4 Introduction
Your Introduction contains background information about your project. There should, at minimum, be a literature review of your construct. This review includes an attempt to locate your construct within a broader nomological network (see Chapter 4). If you are creating a measure of a novel or nascent construct, the inclusion of a nomological network becomes more important, and your literature review should include conceptually similar constructs. In addition to conceptual specification of your construct, it is generally a good idea to include a “Why” section within this section of your tech report.1 What is the impetus of creating the measure (e.g., is there a commercial motive, are existing measures lacking, is there a new technology being adopted)?

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.5 Methods
The Methods section documents the steps taken to define your construct, create your measure, and validate the assessment. This is a tech report component that can justifiably be unreasonably wordy. You are not writing an easy–to–read novel within the Methods section. Instead, you are communicating all of the important considerations and procedural decisions you made along the process of creating your measure. It is ok to “write too much” here – you want full documentation of steps taken such that an individual 10 years from now would be able to exactly replicate your process. At the least, ensure that you cover:

construct identification (conceptual)
item generation process
reason(s) for response scale choice
sampled population description
sampling procedure
survey platform

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.6 Results








Figure 9.4: Appendix Z is coming for you!!! 



The analyses of your investigations go here. This includes qualitative analyses such as content validation and initial number of items generated. Like Section 9.5, it is okay to be overly descriptive within this section. If you feel that the amount or depth of information detracts from reader comprehension, throw the content into an Appendix (Section 9.9). Don’t worry about Appendix Proliferation — if you aren’t sweating the pending instrusion of Appendix Z, you ain’t trying!!

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.7 Discussion








Warning 9.1:  Stay Objective!! 



Smart readers of this section will have their radar on alert for self–promoting smarm and overly–positive interpretations. Your goal should be dispassionate objectivity.2


This section does not need to be very long – keep your interpretation of results to an extreme bare minimum. Your presentation of analyses in Section 9.6 should be sufficient for an informed reader to generate his/her own opinion regarding “how good” the results are. It does not take much interpretive summary by YOU here to raise red flags to the reader regarding your objectivity. Instead, primarily devote the page space here to limitations, implications, and future directions.
Future directions can include plans for futher validation studies — it is ok to propose specific methodologies, constructs, and measures here. Treat these as gifts to graduate students who may have advisors devoid of research ideas. These are your gifts to them

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.8 References
These should primarily support information presented in Section 9.4 and Section 9.6. Make sure to include information regarding your analytical platform (for example, version number) as well as any supplementary capabilities (for example,  packages). There are many different citation formats (both within text as well as within the bibliography). Choose one of your liking and stick with it. This book uses APA 7th edition because that is what Psychologists are expecting to see, although you can use whatever style fits your formatting theme.

title: 9  Technical Report
text:
9.9 Appendices








Figure 9.5: Example Appendix information (Appendix title & substantive content)



All of your raw (unformatted) analytical information can go into Appendices, including any code used to produce the output. It’s quite likely noone will ever read it, but you did it and the odds are technically non-zero that it’ll be someday relevant, so go ahead and throw it in. Don’t go chasing Figure 9.4, but don’t be afraid if it’s looming.
You should have different appendices for qualitatively different content. These are lettered sequentially, starting with “Appendix A”.3 Some individuals prefer “clean” Appendix title pages, such that only the Appendix title is presented and some people include substantive content immediately after the Appendix title (as is done in Figure 9.5). It’s your design choice, but choose one structure and be consistent with it across all appendices.

10.0.7 ANALYSES & INTERPRETATION
Analyses in R 4/5ths Rule – Impact Ratio Differential Validity Differential Prediction Quota Systems Race Norming
The 4/5th rule (i.e., impact ratio) measures the ratio between the majority and minority in employment decisions, based off Title VII protected classes. This is the easiest measurement to see if there are any favorable outcomes between groups.
Step 1. Gather the amount of employees or applicants in that group. Step 2. Gather the amount of employees or applicants selected from the group. Step 3. Divide Step 2 by Step 1. Step 4. Repeat for each group. Step 5. Divide the smallest number by the largest number.
If after your analysis, the answer is above .80, then it is considered that one group is not favorable over another. However, if the answer is below .80, then it may be considered that one group is favored.
